title: My peace I give you (John 14:22–31)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip said show us the Father, and heard that he already had. Your line was seen the father.

A ring. A recipe card. A watch. At a hospital bed or an airport gate, when a goodbye is serious, people often skip the speech and hand over one small thing, something to hold when the person isn't there. At the last supper, Jesus knows he's leaving. A second Judas at the table, not Iscariot, has just asked him a question. Jesus answers, and then he does what people do at goodbyes. He leaves them something. Not an object.
screen: `AT A GOODBYE, PEOPLE GIVE ONE THING.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid." It's a bequest. I leave with you: the language of someone settling what they're handing on. The Greek word is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, which Jews used, and still use, as a greeting and a goodbye. Shalom is more than quiet. It carries the sense of wholeness, everything in its right place, nothing missing. So in one way this is the ordinary farewell any Jewish teacher might give his friends. Then the strange part: not as the world giveth. How does the world give peace? Usually by removing the problem. Pay the bill, end the argument, win the war, then relax. Jesus is about to be arrested. Nothing is being removed. The peace he offers comes in the middle of the trouble, not after it. He also promises a helper, the Holy Ghost, who will teach them and bring to their remembrance everything he said. Then the chapter ends with an odd line: "Arise, let us go hence." And yet he keeps talking for three more chapters before they leave. Readers have long puzzled over that. Some think the Gospel was edited in stages; others think they rose and he went on speaking as they walked. The text doesn't say. In some churches the gift comes back every week: at the passing of the peace, people turn to the person next to them and say, peace be with you.
screen: `A GOODBYE GIFT: PEACE I LEAVE WITH YOU.`
`ARISE, LET US GO, AND HE KEEPS TALKING.`
then, large: `MY PEACE I GIVE UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Notice one trouble you're carrying right now, and don't try to solve it; just let it be there, and in the middle of it, breathe slower. That's the shape of the peace in this chapter: not after the trouble, but inside it. Then picture one person who's carrying something heavy, and if you pray, say his words for them, peace I leave with you; if not, simply wish them wholeness.
Peace. The Hebrew shalom behind Jesus's farewell gift: wholeness offered in the middle of trouble, not after it.
Your line: not as the world gives. Peace in the middle, not after. Day six hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: In many churches, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and others, the congregation shares the peace during the service, turning to neighbors with a handshake or embrace and the words peace be with you.

original.note: Greek: peace. in the Gospels it often carries the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, well-being, a greeting and a farewell.

what it means: a goodbye gift, given the night before an arrest, offered inside the trouble rather than after it.

chat.says: How can anyone feel peace when everything is falling apart?
options: Jesus gave peace not as the world gives: in the middle of trouble, not after it.
Jesus promised peace once the trouble was over and every problem was removed.
Jesus said peace comes from staying quiet and keeping out of others' trouble.
chat.meaning: My peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth. The world removes the problem first; this peace, shalom, wholeness, comes in the middle of trouble.

eirene.meaning: the Greek word for peace in this verse

Iscariot.meaning: the name of the Judas who would betray Jesus

Holy Ghost.meaning: the King James name for the promised helper, the Spirit

notes: John 14:22: 'Judas, not Iscariot', usually identified with Jude/Thaddaeus; the script does not name him further. Confirm.
Shalom as greeting and farewell, and its sense of wholeness: standard lexicon sense. Confirm phrasing.
The 14:31 puzzle and the two explanations (editing in stages; speaking while walking) are both held in scholarship; neither is ranked. Confirm.
Passing of the peace: confirm the list of traditions in howItsDone.
